title: Navigation Hubs and Focus Hubs make comprehensibility a typed structural requirement, not documentation
content:
A.1.2.2.2.25 defines the Navigation Hub Type at the .0.0 position of an Immutable or Primary Document, containing "summarized information and links to the child documents" and, critically, an obligation to "link to the nearest navigation hubs below its position if its Child Documents do not have Navigation Hubs." A.1.2.2.2.26 adds Focus Hubs at nonzero positions below a Navigation Hub, holding detail on a specific topic plus a `links_to` component.

The design problem being solved is stated plainly in the Focus Hub overview: it "can be used to slice up a lot of child documents or a lot of hubs into independent groups, so only the relevant group needs to be read."

This is a real consequence of the Atlas's other commitments. Atomized Sections, one-word Element Annotations, per-rule Tenets, per-action Precedents, and permanent version retention together guarantee an enormous, finely divided tree. A tree that fine is unreadable without an index — and an unreadable rulebook fails in exactly the way the framework fears most, because participants fall back on summaries produced by whoever is willing to write them.

Making navigation a **typed document** rather than a wiki page means it is subject to the same validity requirements as any other Atlas Document, and the no-gaps clause means hub coverage cannot silently break: if a child lacks a hub, the parent must reach past it. Comprehensibility becomes a maintained structural invariant rather than a goodwill effort.
description: A.1.2.2.2.25 and .26 give Immutable and Primary Documents summary entry points at .0.0 and deeper topic slices below, so large subtrees can be read in relevant groups.
